output:
*Interview with Bastien Girard, établisseur, of Le Locle, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Please sit down, Monsieur Girard. I am sorry to keep you up. I must hear everyone who was in the house tonight.

GIRARD: I understand. I have not understood anything since Rosa came down the stairs. Aurèle is dead. I sat at his table and he was insulting me over my watch, and now he is dead. It is not possible.

MATTHEY: I know it is hard. Tell me about the evening, from the end of dinner.

GIRARD: When dinner was over I stayed in this room with the brandy. His good brandy, which he should not have poured for me after what he said about the repeater.

MATTHEY: What was said about the repeater?

GIRARD: I wanted the rights to sell it under my firm's name. He wanted a price I could not pay. I told him at table that it was a fortune for a watch nobody has seen. He told me that a man who buys what he cannot make is no watchmaker. We were both loud. He enjoyed it, I think.

MATTHEY: Did you look at the time while you sat here?

GIRARD: When the temple struck ten, I looked at my watch. It showed four minutes to ten. A merchant notices time, Inspector. I have spent my life looking at watches.

MATTHEY: And then?

GIRARD: I wanted a cigar. I smoke the cheap Brissagos, because the good ones are for buyers. I went out into the street to smoke at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch. The frost was hard and there was old snow in the street. I stayed under the front windows of the house.

MATTHEY: Why did you stay there?

GIRARD: I walk in the cold to think. I did not want to go far in that snow with my boots.

MATTHEY: What did you hear from the house?

GIRARD: The piano started up in the salon just as I lit my cigar, at twenty-nine minutes past ten by my watch. I know that piano. It is a good instrument and it was played well. It was Chopin, I think. It stopped at eighteen minutes to eleven by my watch.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything else?

GIRARD: At twenty-six minutes to eleven by my watch I heard faint quick bells from the master's window up above. Small bells, like a clock striking very fast. The piano was playing all the while. I thought he was trying his repeater. He was always trying it.

MATTHEY: Take your time.

GIRARD: I came back into the house at fourteen minutes to eleven by my watch. The hall clock had just struck eleven. Its face showed two minutes past eleven. I looked at it because it is always in front of you when you come in.

MATTHEY: And where did you go then?

GIRARD: I went up to Félix in the library.

MATTHEY: Why did you go to Monsieur Félix?

GIRARD: Because he owes me money, and I wanted to say so to his face before the New Year. He laughed, the way he does when he is frightened. I was not in the mood to be laughed at.

MATTHEY: Have you any business with the doctor, Monsieur Girard?

GIRARD: Vauthier? He is a good physician, I suppose. He talks as if he were the only man at any table who had read Horace. I do not enjoy his company, and he knows it. He smokes his cigars at my elbow and tells me the Latin. I was glad when he was not at my side.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you wish to add?

GIRARD: Only that Aurèle was a better watchmaker than I am a man. He was arrogant and he was stubborn about his price. But he knew the work. He would look at my watch and tell me what was wrong with it, even when I did not ask. I did not thank him for it. I wish I had.

MATTHEY: Thank you. Please do not leave the town until I have spoken to the others.

GIRARD: Where would I go, Inspector, in this cold?
